29.title: Clothes for the road (Genesis 3:21–24)
29.hook: before they leave the garden, God makes them garments, a first act of care
29.howItsDone: Jewish tradition counts clothing the needy, visiting the sick, comforting mourners and burying the dead among the acts of lovingkindness, gemilut chasadim, understood as walking in God's ways.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the garden and the question, ayekah, where are you? Your line was where are you. When you asked yourself, what did you find? Day twenty-nine.
screen: `THE GARDEN AND THE QUESTION — WHERE ARE YOU?`

segments.voice: Think of the last time someone you love left home. A kid off to college, a friend moving across the country, a parent heading into surgery. Maybe it had gone badly between you. Maybe there were hard words. And still, at the door, you did something small: pressed a sandwich into their hands, zipped up their coat, tucked twenty dollars into a pocket. Welcome to week five, brothers and floods. Before any of that begins, the garden story has one more scene, and it's easy to miss. The humans are about to be sent out. And God does something quietly, with the hands. Today: clothes for the road.
screen: `SOMEONE YOU LOVE, LEAVING.` → `A COAT ZIPPED UP AT THE DOOR.` → `ONE MORE SCENE IN THE GARDEN.`

segments.voice: The garden story ends with consequences. The ground will be hard to work. Life will involve pain. And the two of them will have to leave. But right before they go, there's a single verse. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And the LORD God made for Adam and for his wife garments of skins, and clothed them." They'd made themselves fig leaves, a patch job. Now God makes them real clothes, the kind that last, and dresses them, like a parent dressing a child. Then they're sent out, and the way back is guarded by cherubim and a flaming, turning sword. The door closes. But nobody leaves the garden naked. The rabbis built a whole ethic on that one verse. The Torah tells people to walk after God. The Talmud asks: how can a person walk after God? And it answers: follow God's ways. As God clothed the naked, clothing Adam and Eve, so should you clothe the naked. As God visited the sick, visiting Abraham, so should you. As God comforted mourners, as God buried the dead: so should you. And the Talmud notices the Torah begins with an act of kindness, clothing people, and ends with one, God burying Moses. Kindness is the frame the whole book sits in. There's one more detail. The Hebrew for skin, or, sounds exactly like the word for light. The midrash remembers that Rabbi Meir's own Torah scroll spelled it with the other letter: garments of light. Either way, what goes with them out of the garden isn't only a punishment. It's care.
screen: `GARMENTS OF SKINS.` · `THE WAY BACK IS GUARDED.` · `AS GOD CLOTHED, SO SHOULD YOU.` · `SKIN, OR LIGHT?` · then, large: `AND CLOTHED THEM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Think of someone who's leaving something right now: a job, a home, a relationship, a hospital, a stage of life. Maybe it didn't end well. Picture them at the door. Then think of one small, practical thing you could put in their hands for the road: a meal, a ride, a note, a call on their first day somewhere new. The bell holds the time.
Clothes for the road. Garments of skins, made by God's own hands, so no one leaves the garden with nothing.
Your line: care goes with you. Today, do the one caring thing you pictured for someone who's leaving, even if things between you are complicated. Day twenty-nine.

30.title: Cain and Abel (Genesis 4:1–8)
30.hook: two offerings, one accepted, and a jealousy that crouches at the door
30.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Cain and Abel in the first Torah portion each autumn, and God's warning to Cain, that sin crouches at the door but can be mastered, is often taught in Jewish discussions of free will.

segments.voice: Yesterday: clothes for the road, God dressing the humans before they left the garden. Your line was care goes with you. Who did you send off with something? Day thirty.
screen: `CLOTHES FOR THE ROAD — CARE GOES WITH YOU.`

segments.voice: Two brothers. The older one is a farmer, the younger one a shepherd. One day, each brings a gift to God. The farmer brings some of his crops. The shepherd brings the best of his flock. And God, the story says, looks at the shepherd and his gift, and doesn't look at the farmer's. That's it. No explanation. Siblings have their own versions of this. The parent who smiled a little longer at the other one. The group chat where your news got two likes and theirs got forty. Today: the first brothers, and the thing waiting at the door.
screen: `A FARMER AND A SHEPHERD.` → `TWO GIFTS, ONE ACCEPTED.` → `NO EXPLANATION.`

segments.voice: Their names tell you something. Cain sounds like the Hebrew for acquired: his mother Eve says, I have gotten a man. Abel is hevel, which means breath, vapor, mist. It's the same word the book of Ecclesiastes uses over and over, often translated vanity. A name like a breath on a cold window, and in this story, his life is almost as short. Why was one gift accepted? The text doesn't say. But look at the wording: Abel brought the firstlings of his flock, and the fat of them, the best. Cain brought of the fruit of the ground, with no word about the best. The midrash reads the difference there: one gave the first and best, the other gave what was left. Now the part that matters most. Cain is furious, his face falls, and before anything happens, God speaks to him. Not to punish. To warn, the way you'd warn a friend. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "If thou doest well, shall it not be lifted up? and if thou doest not well, sin coucheth at the door; and unto thee is its desire, but thou mayest rule over it." It's the first time the word sin appears in the Torah, and it's pictured as an animal, crouching outside the door, waiting. But the last words are the hinge: thou mayest rule over it. You can master it. Then the next verse has a gap. "And Cain spoke unto Abel his brother." What did he say? The Hebrew doesn't tell us. The sentence just stops. The midrash fills it in with arguments over land, over where the Temple would stand, over a woman. The text leaves it silent. And then, in the field, Cain rises up against his brother. The first death in the Torah is a murder, between brothers, over a feeling that was warned about.

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Look for one jealous thought you've had recently. Someone's promotion, someone's marriage, someone's easy life, someone's likes. Don't argue with it and don't be ashamed of it. Just name it, quietly: that's jealousy, about that person, about that thing. Picture it crouching at the door. Then notice that you're still the one who decides whether to open it. The bell holds the time.
Cain and Abel. The first brothers, two gifts, a warning at the door, and a silence where the words should be.
Your line: it crouches at the door. Today, when jealousy shows up, name it out loud to yourself before it gets inside. Day thirty.

31.title: My brother's keeper (Genesis 4:9–16)
31.hook: Cain asks "Am I my brother's keeper?" and the rest of the Torah answers him
31.howItsDone: Jewish teaching draws on Cain's question and on Leviticus 19:16 to say that people are responsible for one another; the Talmud's principle that all Israel are responsible for one another is often cited when communities organize help for someone in trouble.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Cain and Abel: two offerings, and a jealousy God warned about before it struck. Your line was it crouches at the door. Did you catch one jealous thought and give it a name? Day thirty-one.

Cain comes back from the field alone. Two brothers went out; one walks home. And God asks him a question, the way God asked Adam in the garden, a question God already knows the answer to. In the old JPS translation: "Where is Abel thy brother?" Again, the question isn't for information. It's a door held open. Cain could walk through it. He could say, I did something terrible. Instead he shrugs. "I know not; am I my brother's keeper?" A lie, and then a question thrown back in God's face. The story, and the Torah after it, spend a long time answering it.
screen: `CAIN COMES HOME ALONE.` → `WHERE IS ABEL THY BROTHER?` → `AM I MY BROTHER'S KEEPER?`

segments.voice: The Hebrew for keeper is shomer: a guard, a watchman, someone who keeps a thing safe. It comes from the root shamar, to keep, the same root the Torah uses for keeping Shabbat. So Cain's question is sharp: am I supposed to guard him? Isn't that somebody else's job? God doesn't argue. God answers with a sound: "the voice of thy brother's blood crieth unto Me from the ground." And the rabbis noticed something in the Hebrew. The word for blood there is plural. Bloods. The Mishnah, in tractate Sanhedrin, explains: not only Abel's blood, but the blood of every child and grandchild who would have come from him. Cain didn't end one life. He ended a world. The same Mishnah, a few lines later, gives the teaching you met a week ago: whoever destroys a single life, it's as if they destroyed a whole world. Then comes the surprise. Cain is punished: he'll be a wanderer, the ground won't yield for him. He cries that it's too much to bear. And God puts a sign on him, so that no one who finds him will kill him. Even the murderer is kept. God answers Cain's question by doing the very thing Cain refused to do. And the rest of the Torah keeps answering. In Leviticus: "neither shalt thou stand idly by the blood of thy neighbour." A few lines later: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." And the Talmud turns it into a principle: all Israel are responsible for one another. Cain asked, am I my brother's keeper? The Torah, and the rabbis after it, keep answering: yes.
screen: `SHOMER — A GUARD, A KEEPER.` · `THE BLOOD CRIES FROM THE GROUND.` · `BLOODS: A WHOLE WORLD ENDED.` · `EVEN CAIN IS KEPT.` · then, large: `NEITHER SHALT THOU STAND IDLY BY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and let your breath slow down. Bring to mind a sibling, or if you don't have one, an old friend: someone who used to be close and has drifted a little. See their face. Now notice what you don't know. How are they sleeping? What's worrying them this month? When did you last ask? Don't scold yourself. Just let the question sit in you the way God's question sat in front of Cain: where is your brother? If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, hold them in your attention. The bell holds the time.
My brother's keeper. Cain's shrugging question, and the Torah's long answer: people are asked to guard one another.
Your line: yes, you are. Today, check on that sibling or old friend. One message, one call. Not to fix anything. Just to ask, and to mean it. Day thirty-one.

32.title: Righteous in his generation (Genesis 6:9)
32.hook: the rabbis argue whether Noah was great in any age or only beside his neighbors
32.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Noah each autumn as the weekly Torah portion Noach, and the rabbinic argument over "in his generations" is a favorite text for study and sermons that week.

segments.voice: Yesterday: my brother's keeper. Cain shrugged, and the whole Torah answered him. Your line was yes, you are. Did you check on someone? Day thirty-two.

The Mishnah counts ten generations from Adam to Noah, and things have gone badly. The Torah says the earth was filled with violence. And then, one sentence about one man: Noah was, in his generations, a man righteous and wholehearted. "Noah walked with God." That sounds like pure praise. But consider the best student in a class where everybody else stopped showing up. Top of the class. Is that great, or just great by comparison? The rabbis noticed one Hebrew word, bedorotav, in his generations, and started to argue. Today's word is what they were arguing about.
screen: `THE EARTH FILLED WITH VIOLENCE.` → `ONE MAN WALKS WITH GOD.` → `IN HIS GENERATIONS?`

segments.voice: Tzaddik. A righteous person. It comes from tzedek, justice, rightness, things set straight. The same root gives tzedakah, the giving you met on day ten. Now the argument. The Talmud records two teachers, Rabbi Yochanan and Resh Lakish, reading the same phrase in opposite ways. One says: in his generations is a criticism. He was righteous only compared to them; had he lived in Abraham's day, nobody would have noticed him. The other says: it's praise. If he stayed good in a generation like that, with no one to learn from, imagine what he'd have been among good people. Rashi, the great medieval commentator, sets both readings side by side and doesn't pick. That's the thing to notice. The tradition doesn't settle it. It keeps both, because both are true of people. Some of us are good because everyone around us is. Some are good in spite of everyone around us. And it's hard, from the inside, to know which one you are. There's another small detail. The verse says Noah walked with God. Later, Abraham speaks of the God before whom he walks. Rashi says Noah needed God beside him to hold him up; Abraham could walk ahead on his own. Again, not an insult. Just an honest picture of a man doing his best. And the Talmud says that in every generation the world has at least thirty-six righteous people. Later folk tradition made them hidden, unknown even to themselves. Tzaddikim nobody would ever put in a book.
screen: `TZEDEK — JUSTICE, RIGHTNESS.` · `CRITICISM OR PRAISE?` · `RASHI KEEPS BOTH READINGS.` · `THIRTY-SIX HIDDEN RIGHTEOUS.` · then, large: `NOAH WALKED WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably, and breathe. Think about the people around you this week: at work, at home, online. Notice how much of what you do is shaped by them. Now pick one right thing you could do that nobody will see. Returning something. Fixing a thing someone else broke. A kind word about someone who isn't there to hear it. Hold it in mind. Don't plan to get credit. If you pray, you can ask for the strength to be good where you are. The bell holds the time.
Tzaddik. A righteous person, from tzedek, justice. Genesis gives the word to Noah.
Your line: good where you are. Today, do that one right thing nobody sees. Not better than the room. Just right, in the room you're in. Day thirty-two.

33.title: The ark (Genesis 6:14–7:24)
33.hook: a box of wood, pairs of every creature, forty days of rain
33.tomorrow: the dove and the olive leaf
33.howItsDone: Jews read the flood story in the autumn as part of the weekly Torah portion Noach; Jewish law also counts care for animals, such as feeding them before oneself, as a duty.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was tzaddik: a righteous person, and the rabbis' argument about Noah. Your line was good where you are. What was the right thing nobody saw? Day thirty-three.

God gives Noah instructions, and they read like a lumber order. Gopher wood. Rooms inside. Pitch, inside and out. Three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, thirty high. Three decks. A window. A door in the side. Then the passengers: a male and a female of every kind of living thing, and of the clean animals, seven and seven, the text says. Food for all of them. And then the rain. The fountains of the deep break open, the windows of heaven open, and it rains forty days and forty nights. The water rises above the mountains and stays for a hundred and fifty days. Inside, in the dark and the noise, one family and a floating zoo. Today: the box that carried them.
screen: `A LUMBER ORDER FROM GOD.` → `EVERY KIND, TWO BY TWO.` → `FORTY DAYS OF RAIN.`

segments.voice: The Hebrew word for the ark is tevah. And it doesn't mean a ship. Look at what's missing from the instructions: no sail, no rudder, no oars, no one steering. A tevah is a box, a chest. It doesn't go anywhere. It floats, and it keeps what's inside alive. Here's a detail worth keeping. The word tevah turns up again, in Exodus. In Exodus, a mother hides her baby from Pharaoh's soldiers, puts him in a little basket daubed with pitch, and sets it in the reeds by the Nile. That basket is a tevah. The baby is Moses. Two boxes, one enormous and one tiny, both covered with pitch, both steered by no one, both carrying the future of the world on dark water. The rabbis also asked why the building took so long. One midrash says Noah spent a hundred and twenty years on it, planting the trees and cutting them, so that people would stop and ask him what he was doing, and have a chance to change. Nobody did. And another teaching, in the Talmud, says Noah's year in the ark was mostly one job: feeding. Every creature, at its own hour, day and night. The hero of the flood spent it hauling food to animals. Later, a Hasidic reading played on the fact that tevah also means a word: step inside the words of your prayer the way Noah stepped into the ark. But the plain story is simpler. When the world is drowning, the task is to carry what's alive.

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one living thing that depends on you. A pet. A plant on the windowsill. A child, a parent, a friend going through a hard stretch. Picture it clearly. What does it need from you this week? Water, a walk, food at the right hour, one phone call? Nothing heroic. Noah's work was mostly feeding. Stay with that living thing for the rest of the sit. If you pray, you can hold it in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The ark. In Hebrew, tevah: a box with no sail and no rudder, built to keep life afloat.
Your line: carry what's alive. Today, give one animal or one plant some real care. Water it, feed it, walk it, notice it. Day thirty-three.

34.title: The dove and the olive leaf (Genesis 8)
34.word: The dove and the olive leaf
34.hook: the waters go down, and the dove comes back with a fresh leaf
34.howItsDone: Jews read this passage each autumn in the Torah portion Noach, and many read the Talmud's teaching about the dove's bitter olive leaf alongside it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the ark, a tevah, a box with no sail that kept life afloat. Your line was carry what's alive. What did you water or feed? Day thirty-four.

Inside the ark, months go by. Then the turn, in four words: "And God remembered Noah." A wind passes over the earth. The water starts, slowly, to go down. The ark settles on the mountains of Ararat. Noah opens the window and sends out a raven. It flies back and forth and never really comes home. Then he sends a dove. She finds nowhere to rest her foot, and comes back, and Noah reaches out his hand and brings her in. He waits seven days. He sends her again. And that evening she comes back with something in her beak. Anyone who has waited out something long, a hospital stay, a hard winter, a bad year, knows what that evening feels like. Today: the dove and the leaf.
screen: `AND GOD REMEMBERED NOAH.` → `A RAVEN, THEN A DOVE.` → `SHE COMES BACK IN THE EVENING.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the old JPS translation: the dove came in to him at eventide, "and lo in her mouth an olive-leaf freshly plucked." Freshly plucked. That's the whole news. Not a leaf floating on the water, left over from before. A fresh one, torn from a living tree. Somewhere out there, something is growing again. So Noah knew, the Torah says, that the waters were going down. But notice what Noah does next. He doesn't throw open the door. He waits another seven days and sends the dove once more, and this time she doesn't come back. Even then, he waits until God tells him to go out. The leaf isn't the end of the flood. It's the first sign that the end is coming. The dove, in Hebrew, is yonah, the same name as the prophet Jonah. And the rabbis wondered why a dove would choose an olive leaf, of all things. It's bitter. The Talmud imagines the dove speaking: better my food be bitter as an olive and come from God's hand, than sweet as honey and depend on flesh and blood. A strange, lovely thought: she'd rather have something bitter and free. Over the centuries, the dove with an olive leaf became a sign of peace far beyond Jewish tradition. But the story's own meaning is quieter than peace. It's easing. Things don't snap back to normal. A leaf comes back. Then the dove doesn't. Then, at last, the door.
screen: `AN OLIVE LEAF FRESHLY PLUCKED.` · `NOAH STILL WAITS.` · `YONAH — THE DOVE.` · `BITTER, FROM GOD'S HAND.` · then, large: `THE LEAF COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of something in your life that has felt like a flood: long, dark, out of your control. It might still be going. Now look, gently, for one fresh leaf. One thing that's a little easier than it was. A night of better sleep. A conversation that went fine. A morning without dread. It doesn't have to mean it's over. Just notice it. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
The dove and the olive leaf. The first living sign after the flood: not the end of the waiting, but the news that something is growing.

35.title: The rainbow (Genesis 9:8–17)
35.hook: God's first covenant is with all living things, and the bow in the cloud is its sign
35.howItsDone: A short blessing from the Talmud is said on seeing a rainbow, praising God who remembers the covenant; the idea of the seven Noahide laws for all humanity comes from this covenant with Noah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the dove and the olive leaf, freshly plucked, the first sign the flood was easing. Your line was the leaf comes back. Did you spot one? Day thirty-five.

The door of the ark opens. Out come Noah, his wife, his sons and their wives, and then the animals, blinking, into a washed-out world. The ground is mud. Everything they knew is gone. And the first thing God does is make a promise. Not only to Noah. The Torah is almost fussy about the guest list: to you, and to your children after you, and to every living creature that is with you, the fowl, the cattle, every beast of the earth. Never again, God says, will a flood destroy the earth. And then God points at the sky after the rain, at something every child has stopped to stare at. Today's word is the promise.
screen: `THE DOOR OPENS ONTO MUD.` → `A PROMISE WITH A GUEST LIST.` → `EVERY LIVING CREATURE.`

segments.voice: Brit. A covenant: a binding promise between two sides. It's a word that runs all through Jewish life. A baby boy's circumcision is called a brit milah, the covenant of circumcision. Sinai will be a brit. But here's what's striking. This covenant, the first one the Torah spells out, isn't with Abraham, and it isn't with Israel. It's with everyone. Every person, every animal, the whole earth. In the old JPS translation: "I have set My bow in the cloud, and it shall be for a token of a covenant between Me and the earth." The word for the bow is keshet. It's the ordinary Hebrew word for a rainbow, and also for a bow, the weapon. Some commentators noticed that a rainbow looks like a bow with its ends pointing down toward the ground, aimed away from the earth: a weapon hung up in the sky. And the rabbis built something lasting on this covenant. They taught that all people, the children of Noah, are bound by seven basic laws, among them not to murder, not to steal, and to set up courts of justice. And an early rabbinic teaching says the righteous of every nation have a share in the world to come. And there's a blessing, from the Talmud, for seeing a rainbow: it praises God who remembers the covenant and keeps the promise. In the story, a rainbow is a promise God made to every living thing, and people stop in parking lots to look at it. It's a promise to everything.
screen: `BRIT — A BINDING PROMISE.` · `THE FIRST COVENANT IS WITH ALL.` · `KESHET — A BOW HUNG UP.` · `THE SEVEN LAWS OF NOAH.` · then, large: `A TOKEN OF A COVENANT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle, and breathe. Think of a promise you could actually keep. Not a big vow. Something small: I'll call my mother on Sunday. I'll put my phone away at dinner. I'll feed the birds this week. Say it to yourself, quietly, and picture keeping it. If you pray, you can offer it in your prayer. If not, just let it settle. A covenant starts with one promise kept. The bell holds the time.
Brit. A covenant, and the first one is with every living thing. That ends the fifth week: clothes for the road, Cain and Abel, my brother's keeper, tzaddik, the ark, the dove, and brit.
Your line: a promise to everything. Today, make that one small promise, and keep it before the day ends. Day thirty-five.

fork.setup: the flood is over and God makes a covenant. who is it with?
options: Noah, his children, and every living creature.
fork.reveal: every living creature: birds, cattle, every beast. the first brit in the Torah includes the whole earth.

original.note: Hebrew: a covenant, a binding promise between two sides.

trapdoor: what you thought: the rainbow is a pretty sign after rain.
what it means: the sign of the first brit, God's promise to every living creature never again to destroy the earth by flood.
what a scholar hears: keshet, also a war bow. and Sanhedrin 56a, where the rabbis draw the seven Noahide laws for all people from this covenant.
